blocks.text: Method 2 for 1,082 Buildings - From 3DBAG Geometry to Material, CO2 and Estimated WOZ Value
1. Summary

This document describes Method 2 as one process: from the measured 3DBAG and BAG data of each building, to its material mass, its embodied CO2 and its Estimated WOZ Value. Part A (steps 1-7, sections 4-11) calculates materials and CO2; part B (steps 8-15, sections 12-22) calculates the Estimated WOZ Value. Section 23 follows one building through every step.
1.1 Material and CO2

This document explains how material mass and CO2 were calculated for 1,082 buildings from their 3DBAG and BAG data: 1,081 demolition buildings plus one added building, Jan Provostlaan 16 in Bilthoven. The result is 1,800,610 tonnes of material and 393,535 tonnes CO2e, reported in 7 materials.

Mass is unchanged by the factors; only CO2 moves. Before 23 September 2026 each detailed material had its own factor and the total was 447,580 t CO2e. The factors are now one flat value per reported material group (section 8.7), which gives 393,535 t CO2e, 12% lower. Steel falls most (156,131 → 132,686 t) because reinforcement went from 1.99 to 1.55 kg CO2e per kg; wood and brick rise slightly.
1.2 Estimated WOZ Value
Every building has an Estimated WOZ Value (Method 2) for WOZ year 2026 (valuation date 1 January 2025). It is a model estimate, not an official WOZ value.

blocks.text: 1.3 How to read this document
Every number is one of three kinds:
MEASURED – read directly from a BAG or 3DBAG field.
DERIVED – calculated only from measured numbers.
ASSUMED – our own chosen value, used only where 3DBAG cannot tell us (construction build-up, storey height, window share, emission factors).

Where the assumptions are: every assumption has an ID. A1-A19 belong to the material and CO2 calculation (register in section 8.1); B1-B12 belong to the WOZ estimate (section 22). In the text an assumed value is marked [ASSUMED Ax].
Section 23 repeats the whole calculation step by step for one building, from the measured 3DBAG fields to the Estimated WOZ Value, so every figure can be checked by hand.

blocks.text: 3. The process in 15 steps
Part A - material and CO2
Assign a build-up profile from building type and age (section 4).
Read the measured fields from 3DBAG and BAG (section 5).
Derive geometry: perimeter, heights, wall lengths (section 6).
Derive floor areas from volume and storey height (section 7).
Calculate component quantities – m² or m of each building part (section 9).
Calculate material mass = quantity × kg per m² of each layer, summed per material (section 10).
Calculate CO2 = mass × emission factor, and group into 7 materials (section 11).
Part B - Estimated WOZ Value
Split the building into its verblijfsobjecten (units), each with its own area and use (section 13).
Check the BAG floor area against the 3DBAG gross floor area (section 14).
Find the buurt (neighbourhood) of the address (section 15).
Calculate the location index of the buurt, corrected for its dwelling mix (section 16).
Determine the dwelling type from the 3DBAG party walls (section 17).
Value each dwelling: buurt reference value x size factor (section 18).
Value each other unit: floor area x price per m2 x factors (section 19).
Apply the age factor and add up the units (section 20).

6. Step 3 – Derived geometry
6.1 Perimeter from the footprint outline
The outline is in degrees. Each corner is converted to metres around the building's own latitude φ (a local flat-earth approximation, accurate to well under 1% at building size) [ASSUMED A19]:
x = (lon − lon₁) × m_lon      y = (lat − lat₁) × m_lat
Each side is then √(Δx² + Δy²) and the perimeter P is the sum of all sides. The outline area follows from the shoelace formula:
A_outline = ½ × | Σ (xᵢ × yᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁ × yᵢ) |

Where the two constants come from: the Earth is an ellipsoid (WGS84, equatorial radius 6,378,137 m, flattening 1/298.257223563), so a degree is not the same length everywhere. A degree of latitude measures 110,574 m at the equator and 111,694 m at the pole, because the meridian curves less near the poles. Writing that exact length as a series in the latitude gives: one degree of latitude = 111,132.95 − 559.82 × cos 2φ + 1.175 × cos 4φ − 0.0023 × cos 6φ metres, and one degree of longitude = 111,412.84 × cos φ − 93.5 × cos 3φ + 0.118 × cos 5φ metres.

So 111,132.95 m is the average length of a degree of latitude over the whole ellipsoid and 559.82 m is how far it swings above or below that average between equator and pole; 111,412.84 m is the length of a degree of longitude at the equator, which shrinks with cos φ towards the poles. We keep only the first term of each series - the terms left out are at most about 1 m (latitude) and 94 m (longitude) per degree.

The latitude formula is right to about one part in a hundred thousand anywhere on Earth. The longitude formula is the coarser of the two because it drops the 93.5 × cos 3φ term: at Dutch latitudes it reads 0.13% short, which on the 38.8 m perimeter of the worked example is about 5 cm. Both are far inside the 1% the assumption claims, and both are much smaller than the uncertainty in the construction build-up.

Worked through for the example building at 52.13° N: cos 2φ = −0.2463, so m_lat = 111,132.95 − 559.82 × (−0.2463) = 111,270.8 m per degree, and m_lon = 111,412.84 × cos 52.13° = 68,393.2 m per degree. A degree of longitude is only about 61% as long as a degree of latitude at this latitude, which is why the two axes are scaled separately before the sides are measured.
6.2 Outline check and correction
If A_outline differs from opp_grond by more than 2%, the building is flagged.
If it differs by more than 10%, the outline is not this 3DBAG footprint. We keep its shape but scale it to the measured size: P_used = P × √(A_ground ÷ A_outline). [ASSUMED A14]
6.3 Heights (checks)
H_max = h_dak_max − h_maaiveld      H_mean = V ÷ A_ground
6.4 Roof pitch (information)
cos(pitch) = (A_ground − A_flat) ÷ A_slope
6.5 Façade and party wall length (our assumption A1)
3DBAG gives wall areas, not lengths. [ASSUMED A1] façade and party walls have the same average height, so the perimeter is split in the ratio of their areas:
L_facade = P × A_facade ÷ (A_facade + A_party)      L_party = P − L_facade
These lengths are only used for the foundation beams.
7. Step 4 – Floor areas

The gross floor area (BVO – bruto vloeroppervlakte) is the volume divided by our assumed gross storey height (floor to floor) for the profile [ASSUMED A2]. It can never be smaller than the footprint [ASSUMED A16].
BVO = max(A_ground , V ÷ storey height)      Upper floors = BVO − A_ground
Check: usable ÷ gross floor area (GO ÷ BVO) should be 0.6–1.0. If GO is larger than BVO the dwelling unit spans several buildings, so internal walls use min(GO, BVO) [ASSUMED A15].
8. Our own assumptions

3DBAG and BAG measure the size of a building (areas, volume, outline) but not what it is made of or how it is divided inside. Everything in this section fills that gap. None of these values are measured for the individual building; they are our own chosen values for a typical building of that type and age. They can be replaced building by building when better information exists.

8.7 Emission factors and reporting group

[ASSUMED A12] CO2 released to produce the material (production stage A1–A3). There is one factor per reported material group: every detailed material takes the factor of the group it is reported in, so the CO2 of a group is simply its mass × that factor. All steel together is 85,604 t × 1.55 = 132,686 t CO2e, and all concrete 1,376,665 t × 0.12 = 165,200 t CO2e. Copper has no factor of its own: it is an installation material, so it takes the Other factor 0.50, while still being reported as its own group. These are coarse working values – the same set the earlier estimate used (section 27); for official Dutch reporting they should be replaced with Nationale Milieudatabase (National Environmental Database) values.

blocks.text: 11. Step 7 – CO2
CO2e (kg) = mass (kg) × emission factor (kg CO2e / kg)

CO2 is calculated per detailed material, then added up per reported material and in total. Because every material in a group carries the same factor, the CO2 of a group equals its mass × the group factor (8.7). The output stores mass and CO2 per detailed material in both kg and tonnes.
12. Estimated WOZ Value - overview

This part describes how the Estimated WOZ Value (Method 2) is calculated for the 1,082 buildings in table method_2, the assumptions behind it, and one worked example. WOZ (Waardering Onroerende Zaken - valuation of real estate) is the Dutch property value used for local taxes.
[IMPORTANT] Model estimate, not an official WOZ value. Official WOZ values are set by municipalities; this estimate is not issued by or taken from a municipality, Kadaster or the Waarderingskamer.

Method 2 values every verblijfsobject (unit) of a building on its own and adds the values up. Dwellings and other units are valued in a different way. All buildings use the same reference year: WOZ year 2026, valuation date (waardepeildatum) 2025-01-01. The total is rounded to the nearest € 1,000.

blocks.text: 13. Step 8 - Split the building into verblijfsobjecten (units)

The BAG verblijfsobjecten (units) of the pand (building) are read with their oppervlakte (floor area) and gebruiksdoel (use). The 1,082 buildings contain 3,907 units; their areas add up to the BAG gebruiksoppervlakte (usable floor area, GO) of each building.
A unit with woonfunctie (residential use) of at most 400 m2 is valued as a dwelling.
A residential unit over 400 m2 (for example a care home or student housing registered as one unit) and every other unit are valued per m2.
14. Step 9 - Check the floor area with 3DBAG

The BAG floor area is used, as it is the area WOZ valuations use. If it is more than 2 times the BVO (bruto vloeroppervlak - gross floor area) measured from the 3DBAG building, the units are scaled down to 2 x BVO: such a difference means units of another building are registered on this one.
15. Step 10 - Find the buurt (neighbourhood)
PDOK Locatieserver (location server): the postcode (postal code) and huisnummer (house number) give the buurtcode (neighbourhood code), wijkcode (district code) and gemeentecode (municipality code).
If the address is not found: the postal code alone; if that fails, the gemeente (municipality) found for Method 1.
If CBS has no figures for the buurt: the wijk (district); else the gemeente (municipality).
16. Step 11 - Location index

A buurt with many detached houses has a high average WOZ because of its dwellings, not only because of its location. The average is therefore corrected for the buurt's mix of dwelling types before it is compared with the gemeente (municipality).
mix ratio = sum over dwelling types of (share of the type in the area x price ratio of the type)
location index = (buurt avg WOZ / buurt mix ratio) / (gemeente avg WOZ / gemeente mix ratio), limited to 0.5 - 2.

blocks.text: 18. Step 13 - Value a dwelling

buurt reference value = buurt avg WOZ (2025) x gemeente WOZ growth 2025-2026 x (price ratio of the dwelling type / buurt mix ratio). This is the expected WOZ of a typical dwelling of that type in that buurt.

size factor = (floor area / typical floor area of the type in the gemeente) ^ elasticity, with elasticity 0.9 for smaller and 0.7 for larger dwellings, limited to 0.3 - 2. The typical area of the type is scaled to the gemeente with the CBS average floor area of its dwellings.
dwelling value = buurt reference value x size factor x age factor

blocks.text: 19. Step 14 - Value another unit
value = floor area x gemeente (municipality) price per m2 x location index x type factor x size factor x age factor
Gemeente price per m2: CBS average WOZ of dwellings / CBS average floor area, WOZ year 2026 (as Method 1).
Type factor: the factor of the unit's own gebruiksdoel (use); a unit with several uses gets their mean.
Size factor: (floor area / 500 m2) ^ -0.1, limited to 0.6 - 1.2: larger units are worth less per m2.
20. Step 15 - Age factor and total
Every unit gets the age factor of the band that contains the bouwjaar (year built) of the building. The building value is the sum of its units, rounded to the nearest € 1,000.

25. Results - Estimated WOZ Value per dwelling type
26. Limits
26.1 Material and CO2
The build-up is a typical construction per profile, not the actual construction of each building. It can be improved per building with permits, drawings or a site visit.
Floors and party wall thickness drive most of the mass: concrete is the largest material.
Buildings without a storey count (BOUWLAGEN_MISSING) are the least certain.
Foundation piles are not included: at demolition they normally stay in the ground.
Emission factors are one coarse value per reported material group (8.7); replace with Nationale Milieudatabase values for official reporting.
26.2 Estimated WOZ Value
It is a model estimate, not an official WOZ value; no official WOZ value was used to check it.
Buurt figures are averages. Condition, finish, plot size, monument status and energy label of the individual building are not included.
The dwelling type from party walls cannot tell an end-of-terrace house from a semi-detached house; both use their mean.
Non-residential units use the price level of dwellings with a type factor; for industry, healthcare and education this is the least certain part.
The size elasticities, the 400 m2 dwelling limit and the 2 x BVO cap are our own choices (B6, B7, B10).
27. Comparison with the previous method
27.1 Material and CO2

The earlier estimate (material_estimation_1081_co2.json, table co2_emission) multiplied the usable floor area (GO) by a fixed kg per m² for each material_profile_id. It did not use the 3DBAG geometry. Both columns below cover the same 1,081 notice buildings; Jan Provostlaan 16 is not in the earlier file.
The previous profiles gave about 2,650 kg per m² for a 1970–2000 house; this method gives about 1,000 kg per m² gross floor area, which fits a Dutch terraced house.
The previous CO2 used 0.5 kg CO2e per kg for sand, gravel and mortar ('overige constructie mineralen'), which made that one group the largest CO2 source.

This method is based on each building's own measured size, so a large building gets more material and a small one less. Both methods now use the same emission factors (8.7), so the whole CO2 difference comes from the material quantities. Both columns cover the same 1,081 notice buildings, so this method reads 1,800,432 t and 393,500 t CO2e here, without Jan Provostlaan 16.

28. Amsterdam government buildings - floors estimated by us

On 2 October 2026, 13 City of Amsterdam (Gemeente Amsterdam) buildings were added: the city hall, the city and district offices, the City Archives and the GGD. 3DBAG gives no number of floors (bouwlagen) for any of them, because it only estimates floors for residential buildings of up to 5 floors. We therefore estimated the floors ourselves.

Floors = volume_lod22 / (opp_grond x 2.8 m), rounded to a whole number, at least 1. This is volume / (footprint x storey height): the average number of floors over the whole footprint, with the 2.8 m storey height of the residential profiles.
These floors are our own estimate, not measured. Each record stores them with bouwlagen_source = 'ESTIMATED: volume_lod22 / (opp_grond x 2.8 m)'.

The Method 2 material, CO2 and WOZ results do not change with this number: the gross floor area is volume / storey height of the building's profile (3.5-3.6 m for these non-residential profiles, section 7), and the BOUWLAGEN_MISSING flag stays, as 3DBAG has no storey count.
For offices and public buildings, with storeys taller than 2.8 m, these counts can be too high: President Kennedylaan 923 is about 23 m tall, which fits about 8 floors, not 12.
